435.title: The true samana
435.hook: what makes a real renunciant, and the jhana similes
435.howItsDone: Meditation teachers use MN 39's four jhana similes (the soap ball, the spring-fed lake, the underwater lotuses, the white cloth) to describe deepening states of stillness, and monastics recall that the robe alone doesn't make the renunciant.

segments.voice: Yesterday: paticca samuppada, and your line, all from conditions. A knot tied by causes can be untied by causes.

Nurse. Coach. Parent. Engineer. Monk. A label arrives in a moment: a badge, a uniform, a line on a form. Living up to it takes years. In a market town called Assapura, the Buddha told his monks: people call you samanas, renunciants, and when they're asked, you call yourselves that too. So train, he says, so that the name is true, and so that what people give you bears fruit.
screen: `NURSE. COACH. PARENT. MONK.` → `A LABEL ARRIVES IN A MOMENT.` → `MAKE THE NAME TRUE.`

segments.voice: This is the greater discourse at Assapura, the thirty-ninth of the Middle-Length Sayings. A samana in the Buddha's India was anyone who had left home to seek freedom, a wandering renunciant. The Buddha lists what makes the name real, one step at a time: a sense of shame and fear of doing wrong. Clean conduct in body, speech and mind. An honest way of living. Guarding the senses. Eating in moderation. Staying awake to practice. Mindfulness in everything, even walking and dressing. After each step he warns them: don't stop here, thinking we've done enough. Then the hindrances fall away, and he describes the deep stillness of meditation, the jhanas, with four pictures. The first is like a bath attendant kneading soap powder with water in a bowl, until the whole ball is moist, inside and out, and nothing leaks. The second, a lake fed by a spring from below, cool water welling up through the whole lake. The third, lotuses that grow underwater, soaked in cool water from root to tip. The fourth, a person sitting wrapped head to foot in a clean white cloth. Each picture is fuller and quieter than the one before. Only when the mind is fully freed, the Buddha says, can someone truly be called a samana. The weight isn't on the robe, the shaved head, or what people call you. It's on what's actually happening inside, through and through, like water in a ball of soap.
screen: `PEOPLE CALL YOU SAMANAS` · `STEP BY STEP, AND DON'T STOP HERE` · `SOAP, A SPRING, LOTUSES, A WHITE CLOTH` · `ONLY THE FREED MIND EARNS THE NAME` · then, large: `NOT THE LABEL.`

segments.voice: Choose one label you wear, friend, parent, professional, kind person, spiritual person, and let one concrete act come to mind that makes it true on an ordinary day, not a good one. Then set the label down, rest in the breath, and let ease spread through the body slowly, the way water spreads through soap powder.
samana. A renunciant made real, not by the name or the robe, but by a mind steadily trained and finally freed.
Your line: not the label. The robe is given; the freedom is trained. That's day four hundred thirty-five.

436.title: Ten courses of action
436.hook: why some go to good destinations and some to bad: ten ways of acting
436.howItsDone: The ten wholesome and unwholesome courses of action (dasa kusala kammapatha) are taught in Theravada, Mahayana and Vajrayana settings as a basic guide to ethical life, sometimes to lay people alongside the five precepts.

segments.voice: Yesterday: samana, and your line, not the label. Only a freed mind truly earns the name.

The Buddha is wandering in the Kosala country and comes to a village of brahmin householders called Sala. They've heard about him, and they come with a question: why do some beings, when they die, go to good places, and some to bad? They're not monks; they're householders. So the Buddha doesn't give them a meditation manual. He gives them a list they could pin to the kitchen wall.
screen: `A VILLAGE CALLED SALA.` → `WHY GOOD PLACES, WHY BAD?` → `A LIST FOR THE KITCHEN WALL.`

segments.voice: In the discourse to the people of Sala, the forty-first of the Middle-Length Sayings, the answer is short: it's because of how they act. Then the Buddha opens it into ten. Three are done with the body: killing living beings, taking what isn't given, and sexual misconduct. Four are done with speech: lying, divisive speech that splits friends apart, harsh speech, and idle chatter, talk that's useless and badly timed. And three are done with the mind: covetousness, wanting what belongs to someone else; ill will, wishing others harm; and wrong view, the belief that actions have no results at all. Those ten, he says, lead to unhappy destinations. Then he turns them over. Someone abandons killing and lives with the rod laid down, gentle and kind to all living things. Abandons stealing. Is faithful. Speaks the truth. Speaks to bring people together. Speaks gently, words pleasant to the ear and going to the heart. Speaks at the right time, about what matters. Doesn't covet. Wishes others well. Sees that actions have results. Those ten lead to happy destinations. Notice the proportions: four of the ten are about speech, more room than anything else on the list. And three happen only in the mind, where no one else can see. So the list reaches all the way in: what you do, what you say, and what you quietly wish. Later Buddhist teachers still teach these ten, sometimes as the ten wholesome deeds: a whole ethics that fits on one wall.

segments.voice: Go through the good ten slowly in your mind: gentle with living things, honest with what's mine, faithful, truthful, uniting, gentle in speech, saying what matters, content, wishing well, trusting that actions count. Let the one today could use stand out, and if any ill will is sitting there, let it soften toward wishing well.
kammapatha. Three of body, four of speech, three of mind: the ten ways, wholesome or not, that the Buddha told the people of Sala shape where a life goes.
Your line: ten courses. What you quietly wish is on the list too. See you tomorrow.

437.title: Dhammadinna answers
437.hook: a nun answers her former husband's questions; the Buddha says he would have answered the same
437.tomorrow: Four ways of taking things on
437.howItsDone: Theravada tradition remembers Dhammadinna as the nun foremost among those who teach the Dhamma, and MN 44 is studied as a compact teaching on self, feeling and meditation; it is cited today in discussions of women as teachers.

segments.voice: Yesterday: kammapatha, and your line, ten courses: three of body, four of speech, three of mind.

A layman named Visakha walks up to a nun named Dhammadinna, bows, and sits to one side. He has questions, hard ones. The discourse doesn't say anything else about the two of them. But the later commentaries tell a story behind it: Visakha had been Dhammadinna's husband. When he turned to the path, she asked to go forth as a nun, and he let her. Now he's the one asking, and she's the one who knows.
screen: `VISAKHA BOWS AND SITS.` → `THE COMMENTARIES: HE WAS HER HUSBAND.` → `NOW SHE'S THE ONE WHO KNOWS.`

segments.voice: In the shorter discourse of questions and answers, the forty-fourth of the Middle-Length Sayings, Visakha asks and Dhammadinna answers, one after another, without hesitating. What is identity, the sense of a self? Clinging to the five aggregates, she says: body, feeling, perception, formations, consciousness. How does that sense of self arise? From craving. How does it end? When craving ends. Then about meditation. What are the formations of the body? The in-breath and out-breath. Of speech? Thinking things over, because we think before we speak. Of the mind? Perception and feeling. Then about feeling. Pleasant feeling, she says, has a hidden tendency toward desire. Painful feeling, toward aversion. Neutral feeling, toward ignorance. Visakha keeps going, deeper and deeper, until he asks what nibbana's counterpart is. And she stops him kindly. You've gone too far, friend Visakha. You couldn't find the end of your questions. The holy life merges in nibbana and ends in it. If you like, go and ask the Buddha. He does, and reports the whole conversation. And the Buddha says: Dhammadinna is wise. If you had asked me, I would have answered exactly as she did. That is the meaning, and you should remember it that way. A teacher saying a woman disciple's answers are his answers. Her words sit in the canon as teaching, with the Buddha's own seal on them.
screen: `IDENTITY: CLINGING TO THE FIVE` · `BREATH, THOUGHT, PERCEPTION, FEELING` · `YOU'VE GONE TOO FAR, FRIEND` · `THE BUDDHA: SHE ANSWERED AS I WOULD` · then, large: `I'D HAVE SAID THE SAME.`

segments.voice: Think of someone who taught you something real without looking like a teacher, a younger sibling, a coworker, a child, someone you once underestimated, and let gratitude come. Then try Dhammadinna's answer about feeling: notice one feeling in the body, and whether there's a lean toward it, a lean away, or a fog.
Dhammadinna answers. A nun's teaching on self, breath and feeling, which the Buddha called his own.
Your line: I'd have said the same. A good answer is good, whoever gives it. Until tomorrow.

438.title: Four ways of taking things on
438.hook: painful now and later, pleasant now painful later, painful now pleasant later, pleasant both
438.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers use MN 46's four ways and its four drinks to help practitioners weigh choices by their results, not only by how they feel in the moment, a theme that also runs through teaching on wise attention and the precepts.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Dhammadinna answers, and your line, I'd have said the same. The Buddha set his seal on a nun's teaching.

Dessert before dinner. The snooze button at 6:40. One more episode at midnight. Every day is full of small trades between now and later, each made in about a second. The Buddha once laid the trades out in a simple grid: four ways of taking something on, sorted by how it feels now and where it leads. Then he matched each one with a drink.
screen: `DESSERT. SNOOZE. ONE MORE EPISODE.` → `NOW, AND LATER.` → `FOUR WAYS, FOUR DRINKS.`

segments.voice: In the greater discourse on ways of undertaking things, the forty-sixth of the Middle-Length Sayings, the Buddha says people mostly want pleasant things to grow and unpleasant things to shrink, and yet, oddly, the opposite keeps happening, because they don't know these four. The first way is painful now and painful later: harsh practices taken up with harm and still leading to harm. Like a bitter gourd mixed with poison: bitter to drink, and it makes you sick. The second is pleasant now and painful later: harm done with enjoyment. Like a lovely drink in a bronze cup, beautiful in color, smell and taste, but mixed with poison. Delicious now; then it hurts. The third is painful now and pleasant later: someone who struggles, even with tears, to keep from harming, and finds that it leads somewhere good. Like medicine that tastes awful, the text says fermented urine mixed with herbs, for jaundice. Hard to swallow; then it heals. The fourth is pleasant now and pleasant later: the joy of a settled mind and good conduct. Like curd, honey, butter and molasses mixed together, given to someone with a sick stomach. Sweet to drink, and it heals too. So the good way isn't always painful; the fourth is pleasant all the way through. But when the choice is between the second and the third, he points to the medicine. The bronze cup and the foul medicine don't look like what they are. Pleasant now isn't the question. What it turns into is.
screen: `WE WANT THE PLEASANT, YET IT SHRINKS` · `PAINFUL NOW, PAINFUL LATER: POISON` · `PLEASANT NOW, PAINFUL LATER: BRONZE CUP` · `PAINFUL NOW, PLEASANT LATER: MEDICINE` · then, large: `PLEASANT LATER.`

segments.voice: Think of one choice waiting for you today, a talk you're avoiding, a walk, a bill, an early night, and ask honestly how it feels now, then how it will feel tomorrow morning. Then rest in the breath, which is the fourth kind: pleasant now, and good later too.
samadana. Painful or pleasant now, painful or pleasant later, and the wisdom to tell which is which.
Your line: pleasant later. And some things are sweet both now and later. Day four hundred thirty-eight, done.

439.title: Examine the teacher
439.hook: the Buddha invites monks to investigate even him
439.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers sometimes cite MN 47, alongside the Kalama Sutta, when encouraging students to examine teachers and teachings over time before placing trust in them; in Tibetan Buddhism, students are traditionally advised to examine a teacher carefully before accepting them.

segments.voice: Yesterday: samadana, four ways of taking things on, sorted by now and later. Your line: pleasant later.

A new boss, on your first day, says: here's how to tell whether I'm honest. Watch what I do when I think nobody's looking. Watch whether fame changes me. Ask me hard questions, and see if my answers hold. Then decide how far to trust me. That's roughly what the Buddha did. He gave his monks a method for investigating him.
screen: `A BOSS WHO SAYS: CHECK ME.` → `WATCH ME WHEN NOBODY'S LOOKING.` → `A METHOD FOR INVESTIGATING HIM.`

segments.voice: This is the forty-seventh discourse of the Middle-Length Sayings, the inquirer. A monk who can't read another person's mind, the Buddha says, should examine the Tathagata, the Buddha himself, to find out whether he is truly awakened. Then he gives the method. Watch with your eyes, listen with your ears. Is there anything defiled in him? Anything mixed, sometimes clean and sometimes not? Or only what is clean? Has he had these good qualities a long time, or only recently? Has fame changed him? Some teachers are fine until they become well known, and then dangers appear. Is he restrained because he's free of desire, or only because he's afraid? And then, ask him directly. A teacher worth trusting will say: my conduct is clean, and that is my path, but I don't identify with it. Faith built like this, the Buddha says, rooted in reasons, is firm. No ascetic or brahmin, no god, no Mara, no Brahma, no one in the world can shake it. That's the twist. He isn't asking for less faith. He's asking for faith that's been checked, with roots of its own, and the teacher welcomes the scrutiny. It isn't cynical. Watching a teacher's conduct over time, in fame and in private, is what turns admiration into trust.
screen: `EXAMINE EVEN THE TATHAGATA` · `WATCH, LISTEN, OVER TIME` · `HAS FAME CHANGED HIM?` · `FAITH WITH REASONS CAN'T BE SHAKEN` · then, large: `INVESTIGATE THE TEACHER.`

segments.voice: Think of someone whose advice you follow, a teacher, a writer, a coach, a parent, a voice online, and run the Buddha's questions gently: what do I actually see them do, is it clean or mixed, has attention changed them? Don't rush to a verdict; there's nothing disloyal in looking. Then let the questions go and rest with the breath.
Vimamsaka. The inquirer: the Buddha's own method for checking him, by eye, ear, time and fame, so that faith rests on reasons.
Your line: investigate the teacher. Checked faith has roots of its own. Until next time.

440.title: Verbal daggers
440.hook: the monks at Kosambi quarrel, stabbing each other with words; six things that make for harmony
440.tomorrow: The god who thought he was permanent
440.howItsDone: Buddhist monasteries and lay communities study the six qualities of warm remembrance (saraniya dhamma) from MN 48 as guidance for living in harmony, especially when disagreements arise.

segments.voice: Yesterday: vimamsaka, the inquirer who checks even the Buddha. Your line: investigate the teacher.

A group chat goes sideways. Someone says something sharp, someone screenshots it, and by evening nobody remembers what started it, only who said what. It's an old story. In the city of Kosambi, the Buddha's own monks split into two camps. The monastic rule books say it began over something small. By the time the Buddha heard about it, the discourse says, they were stabbing each other with verbal daggers.
screen: `A GROUP CHAT GOES SIDEWAYS.` → `KOSAMBI: TWO CAMPS OF MONKS.` → `STABBING WITH WORDS.`

segments.voice: This is the forty-eighth discourse of the Middle-Length Sayings, the discourse at Kosambi. The Buddha calls the monks in and asks a quiet question. When you quarrel like this, are you acting toward each other with kindness, in deed, word and thought, openly and in private? No, they say. Then what do you know, what do you see, that you quarrel like this? It will lead to your harm for a long time. Then he gives six qualities that create love and respect and lead to harmony and unity. Kindness in deed toward your companions, openly and in private. Kindness in word. Kindness in thought. Sharing what you receive, even what's in your bowl, with those who keep the precepts. Keeping the same virtue as your companions, whole and unbroken. And sharing a view that leads out of suffering. Look at the first three. They come before anything about who's right. You don't have to settle the argument to stop stabbing. You put the dagger down first, and then talk. The fourth is so practical: share your food. It's hard to stay at war with someone whose bowl you've just filled. The last, the shared view, the Buddha says, is like the roof peak of a house, the part that holds the rest together. But he starts at the door, with kindness of hand and mouth and heart. The six are often called the qualities of warm remembrance: a recipe for living with people you disagree with.
screen: `ARE YOU ACTING WITH KINDNESS?` · `KINDNESS IN DEED, WORD AND THOUGHT` · `SHARE EVEN WHAT'S IN YOUR BOWL` · `THE SHARED VIEW IS THE ROOF PEAK` · then, large: `VERBAL DAGGERS DOWN.`

segments.voice: Think of a little friction still in the air, a sharp text, a cold silence, a disagreement at work, and picture the other person without deciding who was right. Picture setting the dagger down, your words, your tone, and find one kind sentence you could offer first. Hold that for a few breaths, and rest.
Verbal daggers. Words used to stab, as the monks of Kosambi did, and six qualities that put them down.
Your line: verbal daggers down. Kindness first, and then the talking can begin. See you tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 440 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE GOD WHO THOUGHT HE WAS PERMANENT.`

441.title: The god who thought he was permanent
441.hook: Baka the Brahma believes his heaven eternal; the Buddha shows him otherwise
441.howItsDone: In Buddhist cosmology even the Brahma gods live long but finite lives; teachers use stories like Baka's to show that no state of existence, however blissful, is permanent, and reflection on impermanence (anicca) is a traditional meditation subject.

segments.voice: Yesterday: verbal daggers, and the six qualities that put them down. Your line: verbal daggers down. Today ends a week, with a god who was very sure of himself.

Somewhere there's a person who has lived in the same town all their life and will tell you, kindly and firmly, that it's the best place in the world. They may be right. But they've never been anywhere else, so how would they know? Now make that person a god, living in a radiant heaven so long that he's forgotten arriving. His name is Baka, a Brahma god, and he has a theory about his home.
screen: `THE BEST PLACE IN THE WORLD.` → `BUT NEVER BEEN ANYWHERE ELSE.` → `BAKA, A BRAHMA GOD, AND HIS THEORY.`

segments.voice: This is the forty-ninth discourse of the Middle-Length Sayings, the invitation of a Brahma. Baka holds this view: this place is permanent, eternal, complete. Here nobody is born, ages or dies, and there's no escape beyond it, because nothing is beyond it. The Buddha, knowing the god's thought, appears in his heaven. Baka welcomes him warmly and repeats his claim. Baka has fallen into ignorance, the Buddha says: he calls permanent what is impermanent. Then Mara, the tempter, slips into the scene, speaking through one of the god's assembly: don't contradict the Brahma, he's the creator, the lord of all. The Buddha sees through it. I know you, Mara. Then he shows Baka what Baka hasn't seen. There are other realms, higher and more radiant, which you don't know and can't see. And you yourself once lived in one of them, and have forgotten. Then comes a contest. Baka says: I'll vanish from you. He can't. The Buddha says: I'll vanish from you. He does, and speaks a verse, his voice heard while his body can't be seen. The god and his whole assembly are astonished. Under the drama is the point. Even a long, bright life in a heaven is still a life: arisen, and so it will pass. Baka wasn't wicked. He was comfortable, and comfort mistook itself for forever. Look back at this week: a true samana, ten courses, Dhammadinna, four drinks, a teacher examined, daggers set down. Each pointed past something that only looked final.
screen: `BAKA: THIS PLACE IS ETERNAL` · `MARA SPEAKS THROUGH THE ASSEMBLY` · `REALMS YOU DON'T KNOW, LIVES YOU FORGOT` · `THE GOD CAN'T VANISH; THE BUDDHA CAN` · then, large: `NOTHING IS FOREVER.`

segments.voice: Find one thing it's easy to assume will always be there, your health, a parent, your job, this exact version of yourself, name it quietly, and add: for now. My health, for now. This friendship, for now. Don't panic or argue; notice whether it feels sadder, or more precious, or both, and let it rest with the breath.
Anicca. Impermanent: what Baka the Brahma, so long in his bright heaven, mistook for eternal.
Your line: nothing is forever. Even a god's long, bright life arises and passes. That's a week.

original.note: Pali anicca: impermanent. Baka calls permanent what the Buddha calls anicca.

what a scholar hears: MN 49 shows a Brahma god holding an eternalist view, and the story of Baka also appears in the Samyutta Nikaya (SN 6.4), where the Buddha recalls Baka's past good deeds.

chat.says: Do Buddhists believe the gods live forever?
options: In the stories, gods live long, bright lives, but even they arise and pass.
Yes; Baka's heaven is eternal, and the Buddha agreed with him.
No; Buddhists say the gods are wicked and should be ignored.
chat.meaning: In MN 49 the Buddha tells Baka he calls permanent what is impermanent; even a long life in a heaven has arisen, and will pass.
